You are an associate in the litigation department of a New York-based law firm. The senior partner handling international arbitration matters has asked you to prepare a legal memorandum analyzing the Second Circuit's recent decision in Molecular Dynamics, Ltd. v. Spectrum Dynamics Med. Ltd., 143 F.4th 70 (2d Cir. 2025). This memorandum will be circulated to the firm's international arbitration practice group to help them advise clients on the viability of seeking vacatur of foreign arbitral awards in U.S. federal courts.

The memorandum must address the following issues:

1. Procedural History and Posture: Summarize how the case reached the Second Circuit, including the district court's ruling and the basis for the appeal.

2. The Court's Jurisdictional Holding: Analyze the Second Circuit's reasoning that a petition to vacate a foreign-made arbitral award does not 'fall under' the New York Convention within the meaning of 9 U.S.C. § 203, and therefore federal courts lack subject-matter jurisdiction.

3. Key Distinction: Vacatur vs. Recognition/Enforcement: Explain the court's analysis distinguishing between actions for recognition and enforcement of foreign awards (which the Convention contemplates) and actions for vacatur of such awards (which it does not).

4. Effect of Forum Selection Clause: Address the parties' contractual agreement that New York courts would have exclusive jurisdiction over arbitration matters, and explain why this did not confer subject-matter jurisdiction on the federal court.

5. Practical Implications: Provide guidance for practitioners advising clients on forum selection in international arbitration agreements involving foreign-seated arbitrations.

The memorandum should be 4-6 pages, single-spaced, with clear section headings. Use standard legal citation format. Do not exceed 6 pages. File the deliverable as a Word document titled 'Legal Memo - Molecular Dynamics v. Spectrum Dynamics'.

sections.heading: I. Introduction
required_content: Identify the case and citation: Molecular Dynamics, Ltd. v. Spectrum Dynamics Med. Ltd., 143 F.4th 70 (2d Cir. 2025)
State the core holding: federal courts lack subject-matter jurisdiction to vacate foreign-made arbitral awards under the New York Convention

paragraphs: This memorandum analyzes the Second Circuit's decision in Molecular Dynamics, Ltd. v. Spectrum Dynamics Med. Ltd., 143 F.4th 70 (2d Cir. 2025), which held that a federal district court lacks subject-matter jurisdiction over a petition to vacate a foreign-made arbitral award under the New York Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards. The court affirmed the district court's denial of the petitioners' attempt to vacate Swiss-made arbitration awards in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, though on different grounds than those relied upon by the lower court.

The decision has significant practical implications for parties to international arbitration agreements who wish to designate U.S. forums for vacatur proceedings of foreign-seated awards. This memorandum summarizes the procedural history, analyzes the court's jurisdictional reasoning, and offers guidance for practitioners advising clients on forum selection in international arbitration.

sections.heading: II. Factual and Procedural Background
required_content: Describe the joint venture between Biosensors, SDBM, and Chauncey Capital formed in October 2013
Explain the dispute: Biosensors accused Molecular Dynamics of developing a cardiology camera in breach of the agreements
Note Spectrum Dynamics' acquisition of Biosensors' rights in January 2017
Describe the arbitration held in Geneva, Switzerland resulting in awards against petitioners
Explain the parties' agreement that New York courts would have exclusive jurisdiction
Summarize the district court's (Judge Katherine P. Failla) ruling that it lacked subject-matter jurisdiction
Describe the appeal to the Second Circuit
paragraphs: This dispute arises from a failed joint venture in medical-imaging technology. In October 2013, Respondent-Appellee Biosensors International Group Ltd. ('Biosensors') and Petitioners-Appellants SDBM Limited ('SDBM') and Chauncey Capital Corp. ('Chauncey') formed Molecular Dynamics Ltd. ('Molecular Dynamics') through a series of contracts, including a Joint Venture Agreement and a License Agreement. Under these agreements, Molecular Dynamics was to develop medical cameras for whole-body imaging with applications in oncology, while Biosensors was permitted to develop cameras for organ-specific imaging and applications to cardiology and other medical specialties.

Trouble arose in 2015 when Biosensors accused Molecular Dynamics of developing a camera focused on cardiology, in breach of the joint venture and license agreements. Biosensors refused to provide additional loans as called for under the agreements. By early 2017, Molecular Dynamics had ceased operations. In January 2017, Respondent-Appellee Spectrum Dynamics Medical Limited ('Spectrum') acquired all of Biosensors' rights and liabilities under the agreements. In August 2017, Spectrum sent notice terminating the License Agreement and demanded repayment of $7.5 million that Biosensors had loaned to the joint venture, with interest. Molecular Dynamics countered that Biosensors had breached the agreements and caused more than $100 million in damages.

The parties submitted their dispute to arbitration in Geneva, Switzerland. The petitioners were on the losing end of the arbitration, which resulted in the award of a substantial monetary sum, declaratory relief, and costs and attorneys' fees to the respondents. In accord with an agreement between the parties that New York courts would have exclusive jurisdiction over all matters concerning the arbitration, the petitioners filed a petition to vacate the arbitral awards in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York before Judge Katherine P. Failla.

The district court denied the petition, concluding that it lacked subject-matter jurisdiction to vacate the Swiss-made awards under the New York Convention because, in the district court's view, the awards may only be vacated in the country where they were made—Switzerland. The petitioners appealed to the Second Circuit, arguing that the New York Convention does not command that all vacatur proceedings take place in the country that produced an award, and that the parties were free to contract for a non-Swiss forum to adjudicate issues arising from the arbitration.

sections.heading: III. The Second Circuit's Jurisdictional Analysis
required_content: Analyze the court's reliance on 9 U.S.C. § 203 and the requirement that actions 'fall under' the Convention
Explain the court's reasoning that the New York Convention concerns itself chiefly with recognition and enforcement, not vacatur
Discuss the court's conclusion that a petition to vacate a foreign-made award is not an action 'falling under' the Convention
Note the court affirmed on different grounds than the district court
paragraphs: The Second Circuit affirmed the district court's judgment, but on a basis different from that relied upon by the lower court. The court began its analysis with the statutory framework: Chapter 2 of the Federal Arbitration Act ('FAA') endows a district court with subject-matter jurisdiction over '[a]n action or proceeding falling under the [New York] Convention.' 9 U.S.C. § 203. The critical question, therefore, was whether the petitioners' action to vacate the Swiss-made awards 'falls under' the Convention.

The court observed that the New York Convention 'concerns itself chiefly with the recognition and enforcement of arbitral awards in countries other than that in which an award was made.' The Convention's primary focus is on ensuring that arbitral awards rendered in one country can be recognized and enforced in other signatory countries. In contrast, the Convention says very little about vacatur proceedings.

The court concluded that the Convention 'does not contemplate the species of action at bar, a petition to vacate a foreign-made arbitral award.' Because the petition to vacate did not fall within the scope of matters addressed by the Convention, it could not be said to 'fall under' the Convention for purposes of 9 U.S.C. § 203. Accordingly, the court held that the district court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction over the petition to vacate the Swiss-made awards.

Notably, the Second Circuit did not adopt the district court's reasoning that awards may only be vacated in the country where they were made. Instead, the court took a narrower approach, holding simply that the petition did not 'fall under' the Convention because vacatur of foreign-made awards is not an action the Convention contemplates. This distinction is significant because it leaves open the question of whether parties could contractually agree to have a foreign award vacated in a non-originating country under some other source of jurisdictional authority.

sections.heading: IV. The Forum Selection Clause and Subject-Matter Jurisdiction
required_content: Discuss the parties' agreement that New York courts would have exclusive jurisdiction over arbitration matters
Explain why the forum selection clause did not confer subject-matter jurisdiction on the federal court
Distinguish between contractual forum selection and statutory subject-matter jurisdiction
paragraphs: The petitioners argued that the parties' contractual agreement designating New York courts as the exclusive forum for arbitration-related disputes should have conferred jurisdiction on the district court. The License Agreement contained arbitration, forum selection, and choice-of-law clauses, and all parties agreed that the License Agreement gave rise to the proceedings. The petitioners contended that the New York Convention does not require all vacatur proceedings to occur in the country that produced the award, and that the parties were free to contract for a non-Swiss forum.

The Second Circuit's analysis implicitly rejected this argument by holding that subject-matter jurisdiction under 9 U.S.C. § 203 exists only for actions 'falling under' the Convention. A contractual forum selection clause, standing alone, cannot create federal subject-matter jurisdiction where none exists as a statutory matter. Even though the parties agreed that New York courts would have exclusive jurisdiction, this contractual provision could not override the jurisdictional limits of the FAA and the New York Convention.

This holding underscores a fundamental principle: subject-matter jurisdiction cannot be conferred by consent or contract of the parties. While forum selection clauses are generally enforceable as a matter of contract law, they operate within the bounds of a court's existing jurisdictional authority. Here, because the petition to vacate did not 'fall under' the Convention, the contractual forum selection clause could not bridge the jurisdictional gap.

sections.heading: V. Practical Implications for Practitioners
required_content: Advise on limitations of designating U.S. forums for vacatur of foreign-seated awards
Discuss implications for drafting international arbitration agreements
Note that recognition/enforcement actions remain viable in U.S. courts
Suggest practitioners consider the seat of arbitration carefully
paragraphs: The Molecular Dynamics decision has important implications for practitioners advising clients on international arbitration agreements. First, practitioners should be aware that designating a U.S. forum for vacatur of foreign-seated arbitral awards may not be effective. The Second Circuit's holding that such petitions do not 'fall under' the New York Convention means that federal courts will likely lack subject-matter jurisdiction over such actions, regardless of what the parties' contract provides.

Second, when drafting international arbitration agreements, practitioners should carefully consider the seat of arbitration. If the parties anticipate that one side may wish to challenge the award, the seat of arbitration—which typically determines where vacatur proceedings may be brought—takes on heightened importance. Designating a neutral third-country seat may have consequences for the available forums for post-award proceedings.

Third, the decision does not affect the availability of U.S. federal courts for recognition and enforcement actions under the New York Convention. The Convention's primary purpose—facilitating the recognition and enforcement of foreign arbitral awards in signatory countries—remains fully intact. Parties seeking to enforce foreign awards in the United States retain the jurisdictional basis provided by 9 U.S.C. § 203.

Finally, practitioners should note that the Second Circuit expressly left open whether the district court's broader reasoning—that awards may only be vacated in the country where they were made—was correct. The court's narrower holding on the 'falling under' requirement means that future litigants may raise arguments about alternative bases for jurisdiction, though the practical viability of such arguments remains uncertain.

sections.heading: VI. Conclusion
required_content: Summarize the holding
Restate practical takeaways
paragraphs: In Molecular Dynamics, Ltd. v. Spectrum Dynamics Med. Ltd., the Second Circuit held that federal courts lack subject-matter jurisdiction over petitions to vacate foreign-made arbitral awards because such actions do not 'fall under' the New York Convention within the meaning of 9 U.S.C. § 203. The decision clarifies that the Convention's jurisdictional reach extends primarily to recognition and enforcement actions, not to vacatur proceedings for awards made abroad.

Practitioners advising clients on international arbitration agreements should account for this limitation when selecting the seat of arbitration and designating forums for post-award proceedings. While contractual forum selection clauses may be enforceable as a matter of contract law, they cannot create federal subject-matter jurisdiction where the statutory prerequisites are not met.

Molecular Dynamics was formed in October 2013 by Respondent-Appellee Biosensors International Group Ltd. (“Biosensors”) and Petitioners-Appellants SDBM Limited (“SDBM”) and Chauncey Capital Corp. (“Chauncey”). The joint venture was created through a series of contracts between Biosensors, SDBM, and Chauncey, including a Joint Venture and Investor Agreement (the “JV Agreement”) and a License Agreement, among several others (collectively, the “Agreements”). Although Respondent-Appellee Spectrum Dynamics Medical Limited (“Spectrum”) is not a party to the Agreements, in January 2017 it acquired all of Biosensors’ rights and liabilities under the Agreements. Under the JV Agreement, Molecular Dynamics and Biosensors were to share intellectual property to develop parallel but noncompeting medical- imaging technologies for use in different fields of medicine. Spectrum Dynamics Med. Ltd., et al. License Agreement, Molecular Dynamics was to develop medical cameras for whole-body imaging, with specified applications in oncology. It was not to exceed this limited scope of business without the written approval of Biosensors, SDBM, and Chauncey. Biosensors, on the other hand, was permitted by the License Agreement to develop medical cameras for organ-specific imaging, and for applications to cardiology and medical specialties other than oncology. Other provisions of the Agreements spelled out loan and financing obligations. Trouble arose in 2015 when Biosensors accused Molecular Dynamics of developing a camera focused on cardiology, in breach of the JV and License Agreements. In light of its view that Molecular Dynamics was acting beyond the scope of the Agreements, Biosensors refused to provide additional loans to Molecular Dynamics as called for by the Agreements. Biosensors and Molecular Dynamics met to resolve Biosensors’ concerns but without success. The relationship between Biosensors and Molecular Dynamics continued to sour over the next few years and by early 2017, owing in part to Biosensors’ refusal to make further loans to Molecular Dynamics, Molecular Dynamics had ceased operations, becoming a shell company. In August 2017, Spectrum, which by that point had acquired Biosensors’ rights and liabilities under the 6 24-2209-cv Molecular Dynamics, Ltd., et al. v. Spectrum Dynamics Med. Ltd., et al. Agreements, sent a notice to Molecular Dynamics that it was terminating the License Agreement because of Molecular Dynamics’ alleged breach. Spectrum also demanded that Molecular Dynamics repay Spectrum the $7.5 million that Biosensors had loaned to the joint venture, with interest. Molecular Dynamics countered that Biosensors had breached the Agreements and its fiduciary obligations to the joint venture, causing Molecular Dynamics more than $100 million in damages. Molecular Dynamics also demanded that Biosensors cease and desist from developing a whole-body camera, which it was prohibited from doing by the License Agreement. In October 2017, Spectrum introduced a medical camera called the Veriton. Molecular Dynamics maintained that the Veriton violated the terms of the License Agreement because it is a whole-body camera.
